hook.text: Every text pipeline starts with one small decision: where does one word end, and the next one begin?

sentence.text: Take this sentence. I don't think Mr. Lee's plan will work, but we'll see!

split.text: The obvious move is to split it at the spaces. That gives eleven pieces.

glued.text: But work still carries its comma, and see its exclamation mark, so neither would ever match the plain word.

hidden.text: And the negation in don't is hidden inside a single piece.

cuts.text: NLTK's tokenizer, word tokenize, cuts the way a linguist would.

pieces.text: Don't splits in two, so the negation becomes a token of its own. Lee's sheds its possessive, we'll its will, and the comma and the exclamation mark stand alone.

sixteen.text: That's sixteen tokens. And Mr. keeps its period, right where it belongs.

token.text: Each piece is a token: one meaningful unit of text. Usually a word, but sometimes a number, a symbol, or a punctuation mark.

sent-in.text: One level up, the period itself gets tricky.

period.text: A period can end a sentence. It can also shorten a title, like doctor, or mark a decimal point.

lee.text: Here's a line with all three. Dr. Lee earned two point five million. He smiled. Wasn't that great?

naive.text: Split that at every period, and it falls into five pieces. It breaks after doctor, breaks inside two point five, and never notices the question mark.

punkt.text: NLTK's sentence tokenizer, called Punkt, knows about abbreviations and decimals. It returns three clean sentences.

domain-in.text: And even the right word cuts depend on what you're reading.

tweet.text: Take a tweet, with a hashtag, a handle and a smiley.

default.text: The default tokenizer breaks all three apart. The hash comes off NLP, the at sign comes off the name, and the smiley falls into a colon and a bracket.

tweettok.text: NLTK's tweet tokenizer keeps each one whole.

task.text: Neither one is wrong. The right tokens are the ones that keep the units your task cares about.

case-in.text: But even clean tokens can spell one word several ways.

case.text: To a computer, the with a capital, the in lowercase, and the in all caps are three different strings.

six.text: Here are six words, and six distinct strings.

fold.text: Lowercase every one, which is called case folding, and six become two: the, and dog.

door.text: That's right for counting words. But case folding is a one-way door.

lossy.text: U.S., the country, becomes us, the pronoun. W.H.O., the health organization, becomes who. And Apple, the company, becomes the fruit.

signal.text: For counting, case is noise. For spotting a name, it's the signal.

punct-in.text: Punctuation comes off next, and there's more than one way to do it.

punct.text: Here are three common recipes, all run on one short line.

alpha.text: The first keeps only tokens made entirely of letters. So World is gone, because its exclamation mark came with it. You lose the word, not just the punctuation.

translate.text: The second deletes the punctuation characters. The words survive, but contractions get glued shut: the apostrophe in it's is gone, and so is the one in isn't.

regex.text: The third pulls out runs of letters, and splits isn't in two, at the apostrophe.

look.text: Three sensible recipes, three different answers. So always look at what your cleaning actually did.

order.text: And strip it after you tokenize, never before, or the sentence tokenizer loses its clues.

stop-in.text: Next, the words that turn up everywhere.

stop.text: In almost any English text, the most common words, like the, is and of, tell you the least about its subject.

define.text: They're called stopwords. NLTK's English list has a hundred and ninety-eight of them.

fox.text: Filter a sentence against that list.

removed.text: Five of its twelve tokens drop out, and the seven left carry the meaning: quick brown fox, lazy dog, park.

win.text: For a search index, or for finding a text's topic, that's a clear win.

trap-in.text: But look at what else is on that list.

trap.text: Not. No. Nor. But. Even don't and won't.

review.text: Now run a review through the filter. The movie was not good at all.

flipped.text: Two words survive: movie, and good. A clearly negative review now reads like praise.

custom.text: So for sentiment, curate the list. Start from NLTK's, take out the words you must keep, like not, and add your own noise, like movie, in a pile of movie reviews.

kept.text: Run the same review again, and what survives is not good. The meaning made it through.

stem-in.text: One kind of repetition is left: one word, wearing different endings.

forms.text: Run, runs, running, ran. Four forms of one word, and there are two classic ways to fold them into one.

porter.text: The first is stemming: chop the suffix off by rule. The best-known stemmer is Porter's, from nineteen eighty.

regular.text: Runs and running both come out as run.

irregular.text: But ran stays ran. No rule knows it's the past tense.

nonword.text: Studies and studying both become studi, with an i where the y was, and happiness becomes happi. Those aren't words at all.

over.text: And organization, organize and organ all collapse into organ. That's called over-stemming.

key.text: A stem is a key, not a word. That's fine, as long as you only ever compare stems with stems.

lemma-in.text: The second way is to look the word up.

lemma.text: Lemmatizing finds a word's lemma, its dictionary form. NLTK's lemmatizer looks it up in WordNet, a database of English words.

noun.text: Here's the catch. By default, it treats every word as a noun. So running comes back running, ran comes back ran, and was comes back as wa.

pos.text: Tell it the part of speech, and it knows. As verbs, running and ran both become run, and was becomes be. As an adjective, better becomes good.

know.text: No suffix rule could turn was into be. That takes knowing the word.

choose.text: So stem for speed, when only a machine ever sees the key, like a search index. Lemmatize when the root has to be a real word.

close.text: Look back at the four steps, and each one threw something away on purpose. The spaces. The capitals. The common words. The endings.

needed.text: Cleaning well means knowing what you threw away, and whether your task needed it.

next.text: With the words clean, the next thing to do is count them.
